p.src: Cao Cao fell ill, and no medicine could cure him. Just then Xu Zhi, an assistant in the office of the Grand Astrologer, came from Xuchang to see him. Cao Cao ordered Xu Zhi to divine by the Book of Changes. Xu Zhi said, “Your Highness, have you ever heard of the divine diviner Guan Lu?” Cao Cao replied, “I have heard something of his name, but know nothing of his arts. Tell me of them in detail.”

p.src: Xu Zhi said, “Guan Lu, whose courtesy name is Gongming, is a native of Pingyuan. He is coarse and ugly in appearance, fond of wine, unconventional and unrestrained. His father once served as chief of a district in Langya Commandery. From childhood Guan Lu delighted in gazing up at the stars and would not think of sleep at night. His parents could not restrain him. He often said, ‘Even barnyard fowl and wild swans know the seasons; how much more should a man living in this world?’ Whenever he played with the neighboring children, he would draw astronomical charts upon the ground, setting out the sun, moon, and stars. When he grew somewhat older, he gained a profound understanding of the Book of Changes, observed winds and atmospheric signs, attained almost supernatural mastery of calculations, and also excelled in physiognomy.”

When he grew somewhat older, he gained a profound understanding of the Book of Changes, observed winds and atmospheric signs, attained almost supernatural mastery of calculations, and also excelled in physiognomy.”

p.src: “Shan Zichun, Governor of Langya, heard of Guan Lu’s reputation and summoned him to an audience. At the time, more than a hundred guests were present, all men skilled in debate. Guan Lu said to Zichun, ‘I am young and my nerve is not yet firm. First, I ask for three sheng of fine wine; I shall speak after drinking it.’ Zichun thought him remarkable and gave him three sheng of wine. After drinking, Guan Lu asked Zichun, ‘Who now wishes to contend with me—you, my lord governor, or one of the gentlemen seated here?’ Zichun replied, ‘I myself shall meet you as an equal.’ They then began discussing the principles of the Book of Changes. Guan Lu discoursed without pause, and every word was subtle and profound. Zichun challenged him again and again, but Guan Lu answered as fluently as a running stream; from dawn to dusk, neither wine nor food was served. Zichun and all the assembled guests sighed in admiration and submitted to his learning. From then on, all under Heaven called him the ‘Divine Youth.’”

p.src: “Later there was a local resident named Guo En. He and his two brothers all became crippled in the legs, so they asked Guan Lu to divine the cause. Guan Lu said, ‘The hexagram reveals a female ghost in your ancestral tomb. She is either your father’s elder brother’s wife or his younger brother’s wife. In a year of famine, for the sake of profiting by a few sheng of grain, you plotted to push her into a well and crushed her head with a great stone. Her lonely spirit, tormented by suffering, appealed to Heaven; therefore you brothers suffer this retribution, and it cannot be averted by ritual.’ Guo En and his brothers wept and confessed their guilt.”

p.src: “Wang Ji, Governor of Anping, learned of Guan Lu’s divine powers of divination and invited him to his home. It happened that the wife of the magistrate of Xindu suffered constantly from headaches; her son likewise suffered from pains in the heart; so Guan Lu was asked to divine the cause. Guan Lu said, ‘At the western corner of this hall lie two corpses. One is a man holding a spear; the other, a man holding a bow and arrows. Their heads are inside the wall and their feet outside it. The spear-bearer governs the stabbing of the head, hence the headache; the bowman governs the piercing of the breast and belly, hence the pain in the heart.’ They therefore dug at the spot. Eight chi beneath the ground, they indeed found two coffins. One coffin contained a spear; the other contained a horn bow and arrows, though all the wood had rotted away. Guan Lu ordered the bones removed and buried ten li beyond the city, whereupon the wife and son recovered completely.”

p.src: “Zhuge Yuan, magistrate of Guantao, was promoted to Governor of Xinxing, and Guan Lu went to see him off. One of the guests said that Guan Lu could divine concealed objects. Zhuge Yuan did not believe it. Secretly taking a swallow’s egg, a wasp’s nest, and a spider, he placed each in a separate box and ordered Guan Lu to divine their contents. When the divinations were complete, Guan Lu wrote four lines upon each box. On the first he wrote, ‘Holding breath within, it awaits transformation, sheltered beneath the eaves; male or female, it will take form and spread its wings. This is a swallow’s egg.’ On the second he wrote, ‘Its dwelling hangs inverted, with a multitude of doors; it stores essence and nurtures poison, changing only when autumn comes. This is a wasp’s nest.’ On the third he wrote, ‘Trembling, with long legs, it spits silk and fashions a net; it patrols its web in search of food and finds its advantage in the dark of night. This is a spider.’ Everyone present was astonished.”

p.src: “In his home district, an old woman lost her ox and asked him to divine its whereabouts. Guan Lu pronounced, ‘Beside the northern stream, seven men have slaughtered and cooked it; hurry there in pursuit, and hide and flesh will yet remain.’ The old woman went in search as he had said and indeed found seven men cooking and eating behind a thatched hut; the hide and meat still remained. The woman reported them to Liu Bin, governor of the commandery. He arrested and punished the seven men, then asked her, ‘How did you know this?’ She told him of Guan Lu’s miraculous divination. Liu Bin did not believe her. He invited Guan Lu to his offices, hid a seal pouch and some pheasant feathers in boxes, and ordered him to divine what they were. Of the first, Guan Lu divined: ‘Square within and round without, adorned with patterns of five colors; it holds a treasure and guards good faith; when brought forth, it leaves an emblem. This is a seal pouch.’ Of the second he said, ‘Lofty and craggy rise the high peaks, where there is a bird with a vermilion body; its wings are black and yellow, and its cry never fails to herald the dawn. These are pheasant feathers.’ Liu Bin was greatly astonished and thereafter treated Guan Lu as an honored guest.”

p.src: “One day, while strolling at leisure in the countryside, Guan Lu saw a young man plowing a field and stood beside the road watching him. After a long while, he asked, ‘Young man, what is your honorable surname, and how old are you?’ The young man replied, ‘My surname is Zhao, and my given name is Yan. I am nineteen years old. May I ask who you are, sir?’ Guan Lu said, ‘I am Guan Lu. I see the aura of death between your brows. You will surely die within three days. You are handsome—it is a pity your life will be so short.’ Zhao Yan returned home and hurriedly told his father. When his father heard, he hastened after Guan Lu, prostrated himself weeping, and said, ‘Please come home with me and save my son!’ Guan Lu said, ‘This is the decree of Heaven. How can it be averted?’ The father pleaded, ‘This old man has no other son. I beg you to show mercy and save him!’ Zhao Yan also wept and implored him. Seeing the depth of affection between father and son, Guan Lu said to Zhao Yan, “Prepare a flask of pure wine and a piece of dried venison. Tomorrow, carry them into the Southern Hills. Beneath a great tree you will see two men playing go upon a flat rock. One will be seated facing south, dressed in a white robe, and very ugly of countenance; the other will face north, dressed in a red robe, and very handsome. When they are deeply absorbed in their game, kneel and offer them the wine and venison. Once they have finished eating and drinking, weep, bow before them, and beg for longevity; your allotted years will surely be increased. But on no account say that I instructed you.”

p.src: “The old man kept Guan Lu at his home. The next day, Zhao Yan took the wine, venison, cups, and dishes into the Southern Hills. After walking some five or six li, he indeed found two men playing go upon a flat rock beneath a great pine tree. They paid him no heed at all, and Zhao Yan knelt to offer the wine and venison. So engrossed were they in the game that they drank all the wine without noticing. Zhao Yan prostrated himself weeping and begged for longevity, greatly startling them both. The man in red said, ‘This must have been Guan’s counsel. Since we have accepted his gifts, we must take pity on him.’ The man in white then took a register from his side and examined it. He said to Zhao Yan, ‘You are nineteen this year and are destined to die. I shall now add the character “nine” above the character “ten,” so that you may live to ninety-nine. When you see Guan Lu again, tell him never again to divulge the secrets of Heaven; otherwise he will surely incur Heaven’s punishment.’ When the man in red had finished adding the character with his brush, a fragrant wind swept by; the two men changed into a pair of white cranes and soared into the sky.”

p.src: “Zhao Yan returned and questioned Guan Lu. Guan Lu said, ‘The man in red was the Southern Dipper; the man in white was the Northern Dipper.’ Zhao Yan said, ‘I have heard that the Northern Dipper has nine stars. Why was there only one man?’ Guan Lu replied, ‘Dispersed, they are nine; united, they are one. The Northern Dipper records death, while the Southern Dipper records life. Now that additional years have been entered into your allotted span, what more have you to fear?’ Father and son bowed and thanked him. From then on, Guan Lu feared divulging the secrets of Heaven and no longer lightly undertook divinations for others. This man is now in Pingyuan. If Your Highness wishes to know what fortune or calamity awaits you, why not summon him?”

p.src: Cao Cao was delighted and immediately sent a man to summon Guan Lu from Pingyuan. When Guan Lu arrived and had paid his respects, Cao Cao ordered him to divine the matter. Guan Lu replied, “It is merely an illusionist’s trick. Why trouble yourself over it?” Cao Cao’s mind was eased, and his illness gradually improved. Cao Cao then commanded him to divine the affairs of the realm. Guan Lu divined: “Threes and eights cross lengthwise and breadthwise; the yellow boar meets the tiger; south of Mount Dingjun, one limb shall be broken.” Cao Cao next had him divine how long his line would endure. Guan Lu divined: “Within the Lion Palace, the divine seat shall be established; the royal way shall be renewed, and your descendants shall attain the highest honor.” Cao Cao asked him to explain in detail. Guan Lu said, “The workings of Heaven are vast and obscure; they cannot be known beforehand. In time, events themselves will prove it.”

p.src: Cao Cao wished to appoint Guan Lu to high office. Guan Lu said, “My fate is slight and my features unpromising. I am unfit for such an office and dare not accept it.” Cao Cao asked why. He replied, “My brow lacks the bone of mastery, and my eyes lack steady pupils; my nose has no supporting bridge, and my feet lack the root of Heaven; my back lacks the three armors, and my belly lacks the three ren signs. I am fit only to govern ghosts on Mount Tai, not living men.” Cao Cao said, “What do you read in my features?” Guan Lu said, “You have attained the highest rank a subject can reach. What need is there to read your features?” Though Cao Cao pressed him again and again, Guan Lu merely smiled and made no reply. Cao Cao ordered Guan Lu to read the features of all his civil and military officials. Guan Lu said, “They are all ministers capable of governing an age of peace.” Whenever Cao Cao asked about their good or ill fortune, Guan Lu refused to say everything he knew. p.src: Cao Cao ordered him to divine the fortunes of Eastern Wu and Western Shu. Guan Lu cast the hexagrams and said, “Eastern Wu shall lose a great general, and troops from Western Shu shall invade the border.” Cao Cao did not believe him. Suddenly a report arrived from Hefei: “Lu Su, the Eastern Wu commander guarding Lukou, has died.” Cao Cao was greatly startled and promptly sent men to Hanzhong to gather news. Within a few days an urgent report came: “Liu Xuande has sent Zhang Fei and Ma Chao to station troops at Xiabian and seize the passes.” Cao Cao flew into a rage and wished to lead an army into Hanzhong once more. He ordered Guan Lu to divine the outcome, but Guan Lu said, “Your Highness must not act rashly. Next spring, there will surely be a great fire in the capital of Xu.” Seeing that Guan Lu’s words had repeatedly proved true, Cao Cao dared not move lightly. He remained in Ye Commandery and sent Cao Hong with fifty thousand troops to reinforce Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He in their joint defense of Dongchuan; he also sent Xiahou Dun with thirty thousand troops to patrol in and around the capital of Xu against unforeseen danger; and he appointed Chief Clerk Wang Bi to take overall command of the imperial guard. Registrar Sima Yi said, “Wang Bi is fond of wine and lenient by nature. I fear he is unequal to this duty.” Cao Cao said, “Wang Bi followed me when I hacked my way through thorns and endured every hardship. He is loyal and diligent, with a heart of iron and stone; no one is better suited.” He therefore entrusted Wang Bi with the imperial guard and stationed him outside the Donghua Gate of the capital of Xu.

p.src: At that time there was a man named Geng Ji, courtesy name Jixing, a native of Luoyang. Formerly an aide in the Chancellor’s office, he had later been promoted to Palace Attendant and Minister of the Lesser Treasury, and he was very close to Rectifier Wei Huang. When he saw Cao Cao raised to the rank of king and using the Son of Heaven’s carriages and robes whenever he went abroad, he was deeply indignant. In the first month of spring in the twenty-third year of Jian’an, Geng Ji secretly conferred with Wei Huang, saying, “The villain Cao grows more wicked by the day. Before long he will surely usurp the throne. We are ministers of Han. How can we join the wicked and aid one another in evil?” Wei Huang said, “I have a trusted confidant named Jin Yi, a descendant of the Han minister Jin Midi. He has long desired to strike down Cao Cao; moreover, he is on very close terms with Wang Bi. If we can enlist him in our plot, our great undertaking will succeed.” Geng Ji said, “But since he is so close to Wang Bi, how could he be willing to join our plot?” Wei Huang said, “Let us go and speak with him first, and see what he says.”

p.src: Thereupon the two men went together to Jin Yi’s residence. Jin Yi received them in the rear hall, and they sat down. Wei Huang said, “Dewei, you are very close to Chief Clerk Wang. The three of us have come especially to ask a favor.” Jin Yi said, “What do you ask of me?” Wei Huang said, “I hear the King of Wei will soon accept the abdication and ascend the imperial throne. You and Chief Clerk Wang are certain to be greatly promoted. We hope you will not abandon us, but graciously help us rise. We would be deeply grateful for your kindness!” Jin Yi swept back his sleeves and rose. Just then a servant brought in tea, and Jin Yi dashed it onto the floor. Feigning surprise, Wei Huang said, “Dewei, we are old friends. Why treat us so coldly?” Jin Yi said, “I befriended you because I believed you to be descendants of ministers of the Han court; yet now, instead of repaying your sovereign’s grace, you seek to aid a rebel. How could I have the face to remain your friend?” Geng Ji said, “But such is Heaven’s decree. We have no choice!” Jin Yi was furious. Seeing that Jin Yi truly possessed a loyal and righteous heart, Geng Ji and Wei Huang told him the truth: “Our true wish is to destroy the villain, and we came to seek your help. Our earlier words were only meant to test you.” Jin Yi said, “My family has served the Han for generations. How could I follow a traitor? p.src: Jin Yi said, “I have two trusted men whose fathers were killed by the villain Cao. They now live outside the city and can serve as our wings.” Geng Ji asked who they were. Jin Yi said, “They are the sons of the imperial physician Ji Ping. The elder is Ji Miao, courtesy name Wenran; the younger is Ji Mu, courtesy name Siran. In the affair of Dong Cheng’s girdle edict, Cao Cao once put their father to death. The two sons fled to a distant region and escaped the disaster. They have now secretly returned to the capital of Xu. If asked to help us destroy the villain, they will certainly agree.” Geng Ji and Wei Huang were overjoyed. Jin Yi immediately sent someone to summon the two Ji brothers in secret. Before long, the two men arrived. Jin Yi told them the whole affair. Overcome with grief and fury, the brothers shed tears; their resentment soared to Heaven, and they swore to kill the traitor to the realm. Jin Yi said, “On the night of the fifteenth day of the first month, the city will be ablaze with lanterns as the Lantern Festival is celebrated. Minister Geng and Rectifier Wei, each of you shall lead your household retainers in an assault upon Wang Bi’s camp; as soon as you see fire rise within the camp, divide into two columns and charge in; after killing Wang Bi, follow me straight into the palace. We shall ask the Son of Heaven to ascend the Five Phoenix Tower and personally proclaim to the assembled officials that the villain is to be destroyed. The brothers Ji Wenran shall attack from outside the city and set fires as the signal. They must raise a great cry, calling on the people to execute the traitor to the realm, and cut off the relief troops from within the city; once the Son of Heaven issues an edict and order has been restored, we shall advance upon Ye Commandery to capture Cao Cao, while immediately dispatching a messenger with the edict to summon Imperial Uncle Liu. We make our pact today. At the second watch on the appointed day, we shall rise. Do not bring disaster upon yourselves as Dong Cheng did.” The five men swore before Heaven, smeared their lips with sacrificial blood, and pledged their alliance. Then each returned home to prepare troops, horses, and weapons, ready to act on the appointed day.

p.src: Now Geng Ji and Wei Huang each had three or four hundred household retainers, whom they equipped with weapons. The brothers Ji Miao and Ji Mu likewise gathered three or four hundred men, claiming only that they were going hunting. When all their preparations were complete, Jin Yi went to see Wang Bi ahead of the appointed day and said, “The realm is now somewhat at peace, and the Prince of Wei's might shakes all under Heaven. As the Lantern Festival is upon us, we cannot fail to display lanterns and fires, thereby showing the splendor of an age of peace.” Wang Bi approved his proposal and proclaimed throughout the city that every household should hang lanterns and colored decorations to celebrate the festival. On the night of the fifteenth day of the first month, the sky was clear, and stars and moon shone together. Throughout every street and marketplace, splendid lanterns vied in brilliance. Truly, the night watch imposed no ban, and the water clock urged no one home! Wang Bi feasted in the camp with the commanders of the imperial guard. After the second watch, shouts suddenly arose within the camp, and someone reported that a fire had broken out behind it. Wang Bi hurried from his tent to look and saw flames roiling wildly. Hearing battle cries resound to the heavens, he knew that a mutiny had erupted in the camp. He hastily mounted and fled through the south gate, but there encountered Geng Ji, whose arrow struck him in the shoulder and nearly threw him from the saddle; he therefore fled toward the west gate. A carriage came pursuing from behind. In his panic, Wang Bi abandoned his horse and continued on foot. Reaching Jin Yi's gate, he knocked frantically. Jin Yi, as it happened, had sent men to set fire to the camp, while he personally led his retainers after them to join the fighting, leaving only the women at home. When those within heard Wang Bi knocking, they assumed Jin Yi had returned. From behind the gate, Jin Yi's wife asked, “Have you killed that scoundrel Wang Bi?” Wang Bi was aghast. Only then realizing that Jin Yi was one of the conspirators, he went straight to Cao Xiu's residence and reported that Jin Yi, Geng Ji, and the others were plotting rebellion together. Cao Xiu hastily donned his armor, mounted, and led more than a thousand men against the enemy in the city. Fires sprang up throughout the city and caught the Five Phoenix Tower; the Emperor withdrew into the innermost palace. The Cao clan's trusted henchmen held the palace gates to the death. All through the city men could be heard shouting, “Slay every Cao traitor and uphold the House of Han!”

p.src: Now Xiahou Dun, under Cao Cao's orders, had been patrolling Xuchang with thirty thousand troops and was encamped five li outside the city. That night, seeing fire rise in the city from afar, he led his army forward, surrounded the capital of Xu, and sent one detachment inside as reinforcements. Cao Xiu fought amid the chaos until dawn. Geng Ji, Wei Huang, and their comrades received no aid. Word came that Jin Yi and the two Ji brothers had all been killed. Xiahou Dun entered the city, extinguished the remaining fires, arrested every member of the five men's families and clans, and sent a swift messenger to report to Cao Cao. Cao Cao ordered Geng Ji, Wei Huang, and every member of the five clans, young and old, to be beheaded in the marketplace. He further ordered all officials at court, high and low, to be arrested and escorted to Ye Commandery to await his judgment.

p.src: Xiahou Dun beheaded every member of the five families and clans, young and old, and escorted the officials to Ye Commandery. At the drill ground, Cao Cao planted a red banner on the left and a white banner on the right, then proclaimed, “When Geng Ji, Wei Huang, and the others rebelled and set fire to the capital of Xu, some of you went out to fight the fire, while others shut your gates and remained inside. Those who helped fight the fire may stand beneath the red banner. Those who did not may stand beneath the white banner.” The officials reasoned that those who had fought the fire must be innocent, and so most of them hurried beneath the red banner. Only one-third of them stood beneath the white banner. Cao Cao ordered every man beneath the red banner arrested. The officials each protested their innocence. Cao Cao said, “At the time, you did not truly intend to fight the fire; in fact, you meant to aid the rebels.” He ordered them all dragged to the bank of the Zhang River and beheaded; more than three hundred officials died. Those who had stood beneath the white banner were all rewarded and ordered to return to the capital of Xu. By then Wang Bi had died when his arrow wound worsened, and Cao Cao ordered that he be buried with full honors. He appointed Cao Xiu commander-in-chief of the imperial guard, Zhong Yao chancellor of state, and Hua Xin imperial censor-in-chief. He then established six classes and eighteen ranks of marquises, with the seventeenth rank being Marquis Within the Passes, all bearing gold seals and purple ribbons. He also established the sixteenth rank, Marquis Inside or Outside the Passes, bearing a silver seal with a tortoise-shaped knob and a black ribbon, and the fifteenth rank, Grandee of the Fifth Order, bearing a bronze seal and a looped cord ribbon. With ranks fixed and offices bestowed, a new set of men once more filled the court. Only then did Cao Cao understand Guan Lu's prophecy of fire, and he rewarded him lavishly. Guan Lu declined it.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Hong led his army to Hanzhong and ordered Zhang He and Xiahou Yuan each to occupy a strategic position. Cao Hong personally advanced to meet the enemy. At that time Zhang Fei and Lei Tong were guarding Baxi. Ma Chao's troops reached Xiabian. He appointed Wu Lan vanguard and sent him scouting with a force. When Wu Lan encountered Cao Hong's army, he wished to withdraw. His subordinate commander Ren Kui said, “The enemy has only just arrived. If we do not first blunt their ardor, how can we face Mengqi?” Thereupon he spurred his horse, leveled his spear, and challenged Cao Hong. Cao Hong rode out himself, saber in hand. After three bouts, he cut Ren Kui down from his horse and pressed the advantage with an assault. Wu Lan suffered a crushing defeat and returned to Ma Chao. Ma Chao rebuked him: “Without receiving my orders, why did you underestimate the enemy and bring about this defeat?” Wu Lan replied, “Ren Kui would not heed my words, and that is why we were defeated.” Ma Chao said, “Guard the pass closely and do not engage them.” At the same time, he sent a report to Chengdu and awaited further orders.

p.src: When Ma Chao did not emerge for several days, Cao Hong feared a ruse and withdrew his army to Nanzheng. Zhang He came to Cao Hong and asked, “General, after cutting down an enemy commander, why have you withdrawn?” Cao Hong replied, “Seeing that Ma Chao would not come out, I feared he had some other scheme. Moreover, while I was in Ye Commandery, I heard the divine soothsayer Guan Lu say that a great commander would be lost in this place. That prophecy troubles me, so I dare not advance rashly.” Zhang He laughed loudly. “You have commanded armies for half your life, General. How can you now believe a diviner's words and allow them to cloud your mind? Though I have little talent, I ask leave to take my own troops and capture Baxi. Once Baxi is ours, Shu Commandery will be easily taken.” Cao Hong said, “Baxi is guarded by Zhang Fei, who is no ordinary opponent. You must not underestimate him.” Zhang He replied, “Everyone fears Zhang Fei, but to me he is no more than a child! I shall certainly capture him on this campaign!” Cao Hong asked, “What if something goes amiss?” Zhang He replied, “I shall willingly submit to military law.” Cao Hong made him sign a written pledge, and Zhang He advanced with his troops.
